527.s: Hampton threatened the sidemen over outside recordings; his wife Gladys settled it.
527.q: He put it to us because we had our pianist named George Wallington, who a white guy, he came in the band, and he was naïve. He didn’t know Lionel as good as we knew him. We never intended to tell [him] what our activities were, but he mentioned it one day, and Lionel found out and called a meeting…

527.t: Quincy Jones and the cliques in Hampton's band
527.s: Meeting Quincy, Gigi Gryce and Benny Golson, the two cliques, and the recording with the whole band minus Hampton.
527.q: He was a fine guy. He was straight ahead. I spoke to him on the telephone sometime. He seems to be the same guy. Of course, he’s in another atmosphere now [laughs]. But, he’s still Quincy. He’s not like Mr. Jones, not that kind of stuff. I met Gigi in the band, I met Benny Golson in the band, Monk…

527.t: Recording secretly in Sweden and Hampton's reaction
527.s: Local rhythm sections, sneaking out to a recording studio, and Hampton calling everybody Gates.
527.q: Oh, they played good, yeah! Swedish guys, they were down with it. Jazz has a long tradition in France going back to the 30s. Benny Carter and guys like that were over there a long time ago. They were able to do okay. Of course, we had our guys too. I don’t remember feeling like really in a problem.…

108.t: Antagonism toward Lionel Hampton over treatment of sidemen
108.s: Wilder says Hampton's band was hard to work in, citing how bassist Vernon Alley was dropped with only a ticket home when he fell ill in Texas.
108.q: It wasn’t, no it wasn’t. There were many times when it wasn’t. And the funny thing of it is that my antagonism towards Lionel didn’t come from anything he did to me personally, it was things that they did to other people that you were witness to you know. For instance the bass player, Vernon Alley,…

108.t: Adapting to Hampton and resenting how he treated the band
108.s: Fred Beckett mocks his lead style; Wilder criticizes Hampton and his wife for the working conditions and underpayment.
108.q: I think I did. In fact, I know I did. I had to, because, when I went in, I was playing some of the lead parts the way I had been playing in Les Hite’s band, and Fred Beckett in particular would turn around and say, “What was that?” Literally made fun of it. Then I caught on to the style of their…

454.t: Joining Lionel Hampton and the pay dispute
454.s: Hampton agreed to $400 a week; Gladys Hampton cut it to $125 on the road in Chicago.
454.ch: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
454.q: America loved him, because he was a showman, jump and down, on his drums. He didn't care about his playing too much. He came in and asked me to join the band. Joe Comfort left to go to Lionel Hampton -- Joe Comfort left to go with Nat King Cole. And he asked me to That's when he joined the band.

454.s: Mingus repeats the $400 versus $125 story and says he was never paid for arrangements.
454.ch: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
454.q: No. He's a very dishonest man, and his wife -- he and his wife made millions of dollars off of hiring unknown musicians out in the sticks for little or no money, promise them one salary, get them out on the road and says, Lionel Hampton has the right to promise that kind of money. I was promised --…

400.t: Illinois Jacquet, Lionel Hampton and 'Flyin' Home'
400.s: Williams tells a story of Jacquet asking Hampton for more money over 'Flyin' Home'.
400.q: No, I don’t remember that one.

1022.t: Lionel Hampton personally; playing over him and lead trumpet
1022.s: Hampton at 78 played over soloists, forcing a stronger sound; made Joe play first trumpet, which he failed at; Byron Stripling preceded him.
1022.ch: Lionel Hampton and life on the road
1022.q: Well I never really hung out with him. He was 78 years old when I got the gig. But he was cool man. This was before he had his first stroke. He was still very strong. I mean he, I don’t know how to explain it but like when you stood next to him and you wanted to play the solo, but he was still…

450.t: Hampton's band in Europe and the Joe Glaser meeting
450.s: She plays the Band Box, is invited by Lionel Hampton to Europe, tours with a star-studded band until he fires everyone for recording, then recalls going to Joe Glaser with Billie Wallington.
450.q: In order to get a job in New York, they told me I had to audition for the William Morris company. I said, “But you brought me over here. How can you ask me to audition?” “That’s the way it is.” I said, “I can’t do that. I’ve never auditioned.” That was another little episode. That was at the Bijou…

101.t: Lionel Hampton, his first band after the Navy
101.s: Hampton insisted the public paid to see him.
101.q: Hamp was a masterful leader, and it was a great experience. I – that was the first band that I played with when I came out of the navy. But he was really a staunch believer in the fact that the people paid to come see him, regardless of who was in his band. He used to chew us out on a couple of…

470.t: A short stint with Lionel Hampton
470.s: Baker played only two weeks and part of a tour with Hampton in the mid-1950s because the pay was bad and the personnel constantly changed.
470.ch: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
470.q: I didn’t spend a lot of time with Lionel Hampton. I worked in the summers, two weeks one summer and a part of a tour a second summer, because, first of all, the money was really dreadful. I think you made some ridiculous – he had no per diem, and

491.t: The Lionel Hampton job and quitting over $19 a night
491.s: Hampton's sidemen heard Golson in Atlantic City; he joined in South Carolina, met Art Farmer and Quincy Jones, and left after Gladys Hampton cut his pay to $19.
491.ch: Reflections, marriage and early road bands
491.q: Coles, Cecil Payne, Jymie Merritt, Philly Joe Jones, and a trombone player. I’ve forgotten his name. We were playing music for the show. Lionel Hampton came through town. Lionel didn’t come, but Quincy and somebody else from the band came to see the show. They heard Clifford. They heard me. They…

328.t: Spirit of the Hampton band and Hamp's contradictions
328.s: A strong band with loving sections, led by a showman who wanted to learn and was an egomaniac.
328.q: It was a very strong spirit, very strong. We had – our trombone section was a section that really loved playing together. The trumpet section was incredible. We had a trumpet section that was just – they didn’t have to use microphones. They’d play a big hall and filling the hall up with music. We…

564.t: Leaving Hampton over pay and the Decca record
564.s: He left after a dispute; he got nothing from the record because Hampton held the Decca contract.
564.q: We had a little discrepancy, and I didn’t want to stay in the band and be fussing and all that. No, I don’t need this. I don’t need this. I’m here to do a job. I will do it, and

367.t: Hanging with Basie and Lionel Hampton's dinners
367.s: Young says he socialised a bit with Basie and tells how Lionel Hampton would invite him to dinner and leave him to pay.
367.q: Count Basie. Count was such a nice man too. Count was a, I liked him as a band leader, as well as any man I‘ve ever played with, any band leader I‘m talking about. Count Basie, he was nice, man. Count Basie used to have a good time too, he did everything too. [laughs] But, he took care of business…

233.s: Management resented members recording on their own, which Monk thought unfair to Quincy Jones, Art Farmer and Gigi Gryce; Monk did one small-group date.
233.ch: Leaving Hampton: Europe and Los Angeles

169.t: Joining Lionel Hampton and quitting over ten dollars a night
169.s: Hampton recruits him from the Congo, but pays ten dollars a night, so he quits after two weeks at the Regal Theatre; he recalls Ernie Royal.
169.ch: Hampton, Andy Kirk and Charlie Barnet
169.q: Yeah. That's where he heard me. He said, 'Yeah, Gates, you gotta come with me.' I said, 'All right,' 'so... Me like a dummy, I was saying, 'Yeah, I guess I will.' I figured here's a big-name...
